transcript: It all started in Mar del Plata.
At 17 I built my first product: a games website, which changed my life. I'm self-taught: I read a lot and study online.

And that was my first step toward new experiences, like working at TACH Argentina (2021 – 2022): a digital wallet, end to end. Remote: the back office, the landing page and the app, on web and mobile.
Next, a new challenge: from code to the classroom, at Ada ITW (2023 – 2024): teaching people to code. JavaScript and React: projects, hello worlds and students starting from zero.

From teaching to a big company: Tsoft. First, on Tuenti (2024): gamification you can measure. The roulette and the referrals; then a dashboard to measure referrals, recurrence and gamification. (Illustration with fictional data.)

Then came AI: taking it to production with CompliA (2026), the RAG assistant of Telefónica's compliance portal: artificial intelligence in internal production. I designed and built it. (Demo clip, with sample data.)
At Tsoft, more fronts: a prototype for Supernova Eventos, an events micro-app (with fictional data), and raising the team's level: I trained colleagues.

And alongside, with what I learned on every front, I built a path of my own: Eclipse (in development), Volta (demo), Velmar (demo made for a client), DentalOS (demo), games-market (test bench) and Kinetic Studio (32 trailers in code). All of it, in code.
Every path opened since I was 17. It all grows into the same thing: seeking new challenges.
New challenges are what drive me: boosting businesses and automating hard processes. I'm not afraid of any industry: startups, corporates, agriculture, space, mining, oil & gas.

Technologies, by where I used them. At work: React, TypeScript, Next.js, React Native, Tailwind, Node.js, SQL, CI/CD and RAG with an LLM. In my projects: security (HttpOnly cookies, CSRF, 2FA, Argon2), Python, C, motion with GSAP and WebGL, and tests with Vitest and Playwright. Studying: machine learning fundamentals, AWS and Azure.

An agentic system, split into parts: 11 agents with separate roles. Not a prompt: a system with roles. Specification first, code second; every claim carries its level of evidence; gates with human approval; tested, not eyeballed.
Run of 10/27/2026, all green: Eclipse-Web 463 tests, Eclipse backend 779, internal portal 132 and 14 browser journeys.
Ignacio Gauna. Open to new challenges: startups, corporates, agriculture, space, mining, oil & gas. ignaciogauna.developer@gmail.com · linkedin.com/in/ignacio-emanuel-gauna

method.label: Method
method.title: How I create value.
method.lead: Six steps. Each with something I did, not a nice phrase.

steps.name: Understand the problem
steps.text: Before building, I understand the context and the business. Talking to the people who use the software changes what gets prioritised.
steps.example: In-person day with clients in Buenos Aires (April 2026): demos, alignment and direct conversation about their real challenges.

steps.name: Align and negotiate priorities
steps.text: I agree on scope and priorities before writing code, and I hold the difficult conversations when they're needed.
steps.example: At Tsoft I take part in technical decisions with the team and support people who join.

steps.name: Design
steps.text: I design the interface and the system together: rules, states and limits before pretty screens.
steps.example: Volta and DentalOS: navigable demos with their own identity and labelled data.

steps.name: Build in stages
steps.text: I split the work into small batches, each with its acceptance criteria.
steps.example: Eclipse moves forward in documented batches, with approval gates.

steps.name: Show and validate
steps.text: I show something that works as early as possible and test it: automated tests, visual QA and demos.
steps.example: Velmar: a navigable demo for a client, with sample data.

steps.name: Deliver and learn
steps.text: I ship with CI/CD, document what I learned and apply it again.
steps.example: At Tsoft I work with deployment pipelines, integrations and CI/CD on Telefónica and Tuenti projects.

method.cycle: A loop, not a line: what I learn when delivering comes back in as the next problem.
method.readsMore: See the models and how I apply them

system.label: System
system.title: An agentic system, split into parts.
system.lead: I code with agents, but each one has its own part and nothing ships without a person who approves.

points.title: Not a prompt: a system with roles
points.text: I built 11 agents with separate responsibilities (product, UX/UI, design, marketing, and frontend, backend, cybersecurity, games and trailer architects), with skills that load depending on the task.

points.title: Specification first, code second
points.text: Every change starts with a short document: problem, scope, acceptance criteria and how to roll back. The work is cut into small batches.

points.title: Every claim carries its level of evidence
points.text: I tell apart what I read, what I tested locally and what runs in a real environment. What I haven't tested is labelled «not tested».

points.title: Gates with human approval
points.text: The agents don't publish, spend or change prices on their own. I authorise publishing and spending.

points.title: Tested, not eyeballed
points.text: The main projects have automated tests, end-to-end tests with Playwright and CI that runs the tests and the build. Run of 10/27/2026, all green: Eclipse-Web 463 tests, Eclipse backend 779 and internal portal 132, plus 14 complete browser journeys.

points.title: Visual QA with binary criteria
points.text: Redesigns are compared against the previous state at several widths and with reduced motion. I state the limits: I test in Chromium.

points.title: Cost and honesty as design rules
points.text: No invented testimonials or clients, everything fictional says «Demo», and no new dependency or spending without my OK.

system.limits: What I don't say: that the agents work on their own, that the system has been audited or that a pentest has been done. The backend's database tests run in CI; I did not run them in the run above.

business.note: The examples come from my projects. Where there is no data, I say so; I don't make up metrics.
business.reading: Reading now: SPIN Selling, by Neil Rackham, on consultative selling.

lean.title: The Lean Startup
lean.idea: A new product is an experiment. What you build matters less than what you learn, and the speed that counts is the speed of each loop.

models.d: The core loop: turn an idea into a product, measure how people respond and learn whether to keep going or change. You plan it backwards: what I want to learn, what I need to measure, and only then what to build.
Two assumptions hold everything up: value (does it help anyone?) and growth (how does it reach more people?). Test the riskiest one first.
The smallest version that completes one full loop. Not a half-built product: an experiment with a goal.
With what you learned, decide: stay the course, or change one piece of the strategy without throwing away the rest.
Measure what changes a decision, not what looks good. And ship in small batches so mistakes are cheap and early.

loop.caption: The Build · Measure · Learn loop: what matters is how long each loop takes.

fork.caption: Pivot or persevere: what you learned picks the branch.

apply.d: Every change is a batch with its spec, its acceptance criteria and an approval gate. A mistake costs one batch, not a project.
The site shows demos of the business working before proposing anything: the shortest way to learn whether it interests whoever is looking.

mom.title: The Mom Test
mom.idea: How to talk to customers without them lying to you, even out of kindness: ask your mom whether your idea is good and she'll say yes.

models.d: Talk about their life, not your idea. Ask about specifics in the past, not opinions or the future. Talk less and listen more.
Compliments, generic claims («always», «would use», «would pay») and feature requests without the why. When they show up, go back to specifics.
A conversation is worth what the other person puts on the line: time, reputation or money. If it ends with no next step, it didn't advance.

items.bad: Would you use an app to get more customers?
items.good: How did you get your last three customers?

items.bad: Would you like to see your sales on a dashboard?
items.good: What did you do the last time you needed to know how much you sold?

items.bad: Do you think it's a good idea?
items.good: What did you try to solve this, and why did you stop?

swap.caption: Sample questions for a business owner. They illustrate the rule; they are not a real survey.

steps.d: «What a great idea.» Commits to nothing.
A second meeting, a trial with a date.
An introduction to someone else or to the decision-maker.
A deposit, a pre-sale, a payment.

apply.d: In April 2026 I travelled to Buenos Aires for an in-person day with clients: demos, alignment and direct conversation about their real challenges.

blue.kicker: W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne · 2005
blue.title: Blue Ocean Strategy
blue.idea: Instead of fighting over the same market (the red ocean), create a space where the competition stops mattering (the blue ocean).

models.d: Raise value for the buyer and lower cost at the same time, by changing the factors the industry competes on.
The factors an industry competes on and each offer's value curve. A different curve is a different strategy.
Eliminate, reduce, raise and create: the grid that forces you to stop copying the competition.
First buyer utility, then an accessible price, then cost, and finally adoption.

errc.title: The four actions, applied to Eclipse

eliminate: Testimonials, logos and clients that don't exist.
reduce: Meetings to understand what you are buying: the demo shows it first.
raise: Clarity: price, scope and maintenance in plain sight, never behind a button.
How fast you understand the offer: in about 30 seconds.
create: Seeing your business working before talking: one demo per industry.
A concrete next step: ask for the demo or the plan on WhatsApp.

errc.caption: Taken from the rules of the Eclipse website.

negocio.metaDescription: How I think about the business of a product: model, digital and physical marketing, brand, operations and funnels, with what I did in my projects and three books I use.
negocio.label: Business
negocio.title: How I think about business.
negocio.lead: Who pays, how it is communicated, what leads to the physical world, how it looks, how it runs and the path the customer takes. With what I did in my projects and three books that changed how I build.
negocio.note: Everything here is design and demos with sample data: no conversion, sale or customer is measured. Where there is no data, I say so.

models.label: Business models
models.title: Who pays what, and why
models.idea: Before designing a screen I ask where the business's money comes from and when. Each demo starts from a different model.

items.t: Multi-brand resale with a house brand on the shelf
items.d: The shop resells brands from invented distributors and adds its own. The panel works out margin and suggested price per variant and per brand. To raise the basket: a discount for taking products from three categories, goal-based packs and gift cards, all simulated.

items.t: Made to order: profit comes from the recipe
items.d: Every product is made to order and personalised. The panel models inputs per unit, machine and hand minutes, margin and suggested price; moving an order to the machine deducts inputs.

items.t: The venue's subscription, no commission per order
items.d: The order is not paid inside the app: it is paid at the till or on the venue's card terminal. Eclipse charges a monthly subscription to the venue, in three levels that stack. No venue uses it yet.

The landing page shows demos by industry; whoever writes gets a demo of their business and a written proposal. The project starts with the deposit: a database trigger rejects one with no deposit paid. Support exists only with a maintenance contract. No customers yet.

volta.c: Profit: price minus supplier and packaging cost.

velmar.c: Profit per recipe: inputs and working minutes.

lucero.c: The only payment in the system is the venue's subscription.

eclipse.c: The project starts with the deposit; no amounts on this page.

digital.label: Digital marketing
digital.title: Write when there is a reason
digital.idea: The digital marketing I designed starts from a fact about the customer (an order that changed state, a product running out, a date) and lets a person decide whether it is sent.

items.d: 12 messages by order state, with the data already filled in and a WhatsApp link. They are edited in the panel and nothing is sent on its own: a person sends it. Reorder works out who to write to about 5 days before a pack runs out, with a link that loads the bag. Volta also turns 17 commercial dates into campaigns, each with its coupon.

items.t: Commercial dates and a wheel that expires
items.d: Sixteen themes by date (Mother's Day, Black Friday, Christmas…) change palette, banner, loading screen and coupon. The eight-slice wheel gives a single-use coupon that expires. Sending is simulated.

The prize wheel appears as soon as the menu opens, one spin per visit; the prize comes with a code the waiter checks in person. Special dates change palette and decoration, never prices. The demo has no campaigns to the diner.

Four computed segments: pending check-ups, quotes with no answer, enquiries with no appointment and cancelled appointments. The audience leaves out whoever asked to opt out and whoever already got 2 messages in 30 days, and a check rejects invented urgency, fear and discounts. Sending is simulated.
The internal portal works out what to do with each prospect: call the same day they reply, send the proposal within 24 hours and remind them at 2, 5 and 9 days. The system sends nothing on its own.

aud.title: An audience that shrinks out of respect
steps: Minus whoever hit 2 messages in 30 days
aud.caption: A DentalOS campaign (demo). The width is illustrative: there are no figures, and the list is ordered by ID, never by profitability.

physical.label: Physical marketing
physical.title: Let the physical lead to the digital
physical.idea: A QR, a plate or a counter is marketing if it takes the person to the next step in one gesture. The repos have four; there is no real signage or packaging, and I say so.

items.d: The QR opens that table's menu. Eclipse Academy's guide says how to place it: at eye height, with one sentence beside it, printed matte and checked every week. The wheel closes the circle: the prize comes with a code the waiter checks at the table.

items.t: NFC plate with the customer's link
items.d: A Velmar product: a printed plate with the image the customer picks and an NFC chip that opens the link they want (Instagram, WhatsApp, a menu). It is physical marketing for their own business.
The employee shows a QR of their booking and the organiser registers entry with the camera or a code. In the demo the QR is a reference to the sample booking and does not validate real entries.
Pick-up at the shop with a code, a counter with sales and an end-of-day close, and samples and a brand shaker as prizes of the wheel and the club levels.

brand.label: Branding
brand.title: A brand is decisions
brand.idea: The logo comes last. First I decide the tone, the palette with its use and what changes from one client to another. The visual detail of each brand is in the Brand Lab.

items.d: Everything about the brand comes from one file per client: name, palette, type and logo. A test forbids typing «Volta» by hand in the code and a check reviews AA contrast; that is how another demo is prepared in about 15 minutes.

items.t: A provisional palette, said as such

«Warm clinical editorial», chosen on 17/10/2026 among proposals, with two corrections. The children's characters have cosmetic gamification, with no prizes tied to treatments.

items.t: An invented venue that does not resemble a real one
items.d: A wine-and-cream palette and the «Demo» label everywhere, without resembling a real brand.

Amber on night, the eclipse as a glyph and the project's five stages as phases of the eclipse. A premium, confident, concrete tone with short sentences: Rioplatense Spanish, direct English and Brazilian Portuguese.

ops.label: Operations
ops.title: A journey with states
ops.idea: In each demo, an order or an appointment goes through states that a single function validates: nobody skips a step and whoever decides is recorded.

items.t: Lots with expiry and a check before dispatch
items.d: The lot that expires first goes out first (FEFO), with a warning under 60 days and clearance with ready-made actions. An order does not become «Ready» without the lots confirmed, and a receipt never pays: it is approved after seeing the money.
To make, On the machine, Finishing and Ready, with the preview approved; moving to the machine deducts inputs. The calendar has capacity per day, holidays and is rescheduled by dragging.

When a slot frees up, a vacancy task is created and it is offered to the waiting list. The offer is held for a while, can be declined with no penalty and is never offered again. Offers are slots, not discounts.
The order moves from sent to kitchen, ready and delivered, only forwards. A dish marked «Sold out» stops showing for the diner at once.

Each event has up to 24 sessions with their own capacity; capacity cannot drop below the sign-ups and sessions with bookings cannot be deleted. Without a server, capacity across devices cannot be guaranteed.

funnels.legend: A path designed and navigable in the demo. It is not measured: there are no conversion figures, and the width of each bar is only illustrative.
